title: SAI 1 — System Architecture and Integration (Complete Review)
subject: System Architecture and Integration 1 (ITNET312-T)
summary: A comprehensive examination built from the SAI 1 reviewer (Lessons L2–L8). It covers enterprise architecture components and frameworks (Zachman, TOGAF, FEAF, Gartner), developing and using an EA, service-oriented architecture, integration technology (XML and web services), application integration styles, and enterprise integration best practices. Each chapter offers ~30 challenging questions with timed and untimed modes.

chapters.title: L2 — Enterprise Architecture Components
chapters.description: EA implementation methodology, frameworks (Zachman, TOGAF, FEAF, Gartner), the four core architectural domains, artifacts, and cross-layer traceability.

questions.question: Which statement best describes an EA Implementation Methodology?
choices: A structured set of tools, models, and guidelines used to design an architecture
A classification schema that organizes architectural artifacts into a grid
A list of approved hardware and software standards for an enterprise
A detailed, step-by-step approach for establishing and managing an EA program
questions.explanation: The EA Implementation Methodology is a detailed, step-by-step approach describing how an EA program is established, developed, managed, maintained, and used.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key benefit of using a structured EA implementation methodology?
choices: It eliminates the need for documentation
It provides clear direction for the EA's scope and goals
It replaces the organization's governance structure
It guarantees that all projects are completed on budget
questions.explanation: One of the six key benefits is clear direction: defining the EA's scope, goals, and overall approach.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six FEAF reference models?
questions.explanation: FEAF's six reference models are PRM, DRM, SRM, BRM, ARM, and TRM. There is no Network Reference Model.

questions.question: In the four phases of EA implementation, which phase involves selecting the EA documentation framework and establishing an EA repository?
choices: Defining the scope, goals, and overall approach
Phase II — Framework and Tool Selection
Phase IV — Use and Maintain the EA
questions.explanation: Phase II, Framework and Tool Selection, includes identifying Lines of Business and Crosscuts, selecting documentation methods and tools, and establishing the EA repository.

questions.question: Every cell in the Zachman Framework represents a unique intersection of a column and a row. To what does each cell correspond?
choices: A phase in the EA implementation cycle
A specific architectural artifact or model
questions.explanation: Each of the 36 cells represents a specific artifact or model relevant to that intersection of perspective (row) and focus (column).

questions.question: An enterprise needs to organize and classify its EA information using a framework that acts as a reference checklist rather than a step-by-step process. Which framework best fits this need?
questions.explanation: The comparison table states that Zachman is the suitable framework when there is a need to organize and classify EA information.

questions.question: Which category of artifacts answers the question, 'What inventory do we have?'
questions.explanation: Catalogs are hierarchical lists or inventories of things; they answer 'What inventory do we have?'

questions.question: A planning team wants to assess the impact of retiring an AWS server instance on business processes. Which part of cross-layer traceability should it inspect FIRST to understand the disruption?
choices: The Business layer to review capability maps
The Data layer to review ERDs
The Technology layer to review deployment diagrams
questions.explanation: An AWS server belongs to the Technology layer, so network topology and deployment diagrams there reveal which applications, data entities, and processes depend on it.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an EA methodology from an EA framework?
choices: A methodology answers HOW the EA program is managed; a framework defines WHAT structure organizes it
A methodology and a framework both focus exclusively on documenting artifacts
A framework is used by public agencies, while a methodology is used only by private firms
A methodology defines WHAT structure organizes the EA; a framework defines HOW it is managed
questions.explanation: An EA Implementation Methodology answers HOW the EA program is established and managed, while an EA Framework defines WHAT structure is used to organize the EA.

questions.question: Which ADM phase focuses on defining the goals and scope of the architecture effort and creating the overall architecture vision?
questions.explanation: Phase A, Architecture Vision, defines goals and scope, identifies stakeholders, and creates the overall architecture vision.

questions.question: Which EA framework was developed by the U.S. Federal Government for public-sector use?
questions.explanation: FEAF, the Federal Enterprise Architecture Framework, was developed by the U.S. Federal Government to organize and manage enterprise architecture.

questions.question: Which FEAF reference model organizes IT services and application components that support business functions?
questions.explanation: ARM, the Application Reference Model, organizes IT services and application components that support business functions.

questions.question: A systems architect claims the Zachman Framework is a methodology for developing enterprise architectures. How should this claim be evaluated?
choices: Incorrect, because the Zachman Framework is a classification schema, not a methodology
Incorrect, because the Zachman Framework only covers technology architecture
Correct, because it defines implementation steps in sequence
Correct, because it replaced earlier methodologies like ADM
questions.explanation: The Zachman Framework is not a methodology; it is a classification schema used as a reference or checklist for organizing architectural artifacts.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the challenges associated with using an EA implementation methodology?
questions.explanation: Challenges include complexity, governance difficulties, requirements gaps, implementation problems, and maintenance issues.

questions.question: A company needs a detailed, structured process for developing its enterprise architecture rather than a classification schema. Which framework should it use?
questions.explanation: The comparison table states that TOGAF is suitable when there is a need for a detailed EA development process.

questions.question: Which ADM phase monitors implementation, checks architecture compliance, and manages implementation issues?
questions.explanation: Phase G, Implementation Governance, monitors implementation, checks architecture compliance, and manages implementation issues.

questions.question: Which architectural domain is described as the foundation of the EA framework?
questions.explanation: Business Architecture is the foundation of the EA framework and defines strategy, governance, structure, and key business processes.

questions.question: Which of the following artifacts would best display the relationships and cardinality among data entities?
questions.explanation: An Entity-Relationship Diagram is a Data-layer Diagram that visually models data entities and their relationships and cardinality.

questions.question: Which FEAF reference model measures how well an organization and its IT systems achieve strategic goals and desired outcomes?
questions.explanation: PRM, the Performance Reference Model, measures how well the organization and its IT systems achieve strategic goals and outcomes.

questions.question: In the Zachman Framework, which row represents the perspective of the 'Enterprise (Actual System)'?
questions.explanation: The six rows are Planner, Owner, Designer, Builder, Sub-Contractor, and Enterprise (Actual System).

questions.question: Which statement best describes the role of Requirements Management within the TOGAF ADM cycle?
choices: It is applied only once after Phase H ends
It operates only during Phase A, Architecture Vision
It operates throughout all ADM phases and tracks changing requirements
It replaces the Preliminary Phase entirely
questions.explanation: Requirements Management operates throughout all ADM phases, tracking, evaluating, and managing changing requirements.

questions.question: The technology layer of the EA framework answers which question?
choices: What information does the enterprise need to operate?
What infrastructure is required to run applications securely?
What does the business do to achieve its goals?
What software applications are needed to automate processes?
questions.explanation: Technology Architecture answers, 'What physical and virtual infrastructure is required to run the application architecture securely and scalably?'

questions.question: Which phase of the EA implementation develops future operating scenarios and defines future planning assumptions?
choices: Phase IV — Use and Maintain the EA
Phase III — Documentation of the EA
Phase II — Framework and Tool Selection
questions.explanation: Phase III, Documentation of the EA, includes developing future operating scenarios, defining future planning assumptions, and documenting the future state.

questions.question: Which FEAF reference model defines security-related capabilities, controls, and requirements for protecting enterprise information?
questions.explanation: SRM, the Security Reference Model, defines security-related capabilities, controls, and requirements for protecting enterprise systems and information.

questions.question: Which ADM phase identifies possible solutions, groups changes into projects, and defines the implementation approach?
questions.explanation: Phase E, Opportunities & Solutions, identifies possible solutions, groups changes into projects, and defines the implementation approach.

questions.question: Which chain represents the correct cross-layer traceability order that enables impact analysis?
questions.explanation: Traceability runs Business -> Data -> Application -> Technology so every technical asset maps back to a business need.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about the Gartner EA methodology?
choices: It is mandatory for U.S. government agencies
It views EA as a continuous process of change and improvement
It views EA as a one-time project completed at implementation
It focuses purely on technology rather than business outcomes
questions.explanation: Gartner views Enterprise Architecture as a continuous process of change and improvement, not a one-time project.

questions.question: Which pair of Zachman Framework columns is correctly identified?
choices: Who — addresses how the work is performed
When — identifies the people and actors
What — answers what data or things exist
questions.explanation: The columns are the interrogatives What, How, Where, Who, When, Why. 'What' focuses on the data or physical things.

questions.question: Which artifact category is an Application-to-Function Matrix an example of?
questions.explanation: Matrices are grids that show the relationship between two or more architectural elements; the Application-to-Function Matrix is a listed example.

questions.question: Why does the reference describe siloed or disconnected artifacts as a critical pitfall in EA?
choices: They are cheaper to produce than integrated models
They reduce the number of approved tools
They lose alignment between strategic goals and technical execution
They prevent stakeholders from joining review meetings
questions.explanation: When architectural components are isolated, organizations lose alignment between strategic goals and technical execution.

chapters.title: L3 — Developing an Enterprise Architecture
chapters.description: Current and future architectural views, documentation techniques (EACR, IDEF-O, ERDs), CONOPS scenarios, future artifact levels, freeze periods, and the EA Management Plan.

questions.question: Why does the reference argue that documentation must come before planning?
choices: Because stakeholders require blueprints before operational data
Because auditors prefer future scenarios over current records
Because planning documents are shorter and easier to review
Because plans built without an accurate baseline underestimate cost, timeline, and complexity
questions.explanation: Plans built without an accurate baseline tend to underestimate cost, timeline, and complexity, so planning starts with an accurate assessment of the current situation.

questions.question: Systems and processes change regularly, but documentation is often updated far less frequently. What does this produce?
choices: A gap between documentation and reality
questions.explanation: Because documentation is often treated as a one-time deliverable, documentation and reality drift apart over time.

questions.question: Which stakeholder group needs a documented record of what changed, when, and why?
questions.explanation: Audit and Compliance need a documented record of what changed, when, and why, while technical staff need accurate detail and leadership needs comparable information.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'As-Is' or current architectural view?
choices: A scenario of worst-case operating conditions
A snapshot of the company's technology and processes right now
A design of the target systems five years ahead
A list of approved cloud vendors
questions.explanation: Current Architectural Views are like taking a complete snapshot of a company's technology and processes right now.

questions.question: An EA Change Request (EACR) primarily helps companies to:
choices: Select new hardware for the data center
Update systems smoothly with an archived history for implementers
questions.explanation: An EACR is the standard format used to update systems smoothly, and archiving these requests creates a history guide for developers.

questions.question: In an IDEF-O diagram, which element represents the 'Controls' or rules to follow?
choices: The inputs that enter the function
The outputs produced by the function
The guidelines constraining how the activity runs
questions.explanation: IDEF-O explicitly defines 'Controls' (rules to follow) and 'Mechanisms' (tools to use), with inputs and outputs shown clearly.

questions.question: What does the tech inventory in EA enable leadership to do?
choices: Justify upgrades with concrete proof when authorizing purchases
Rewrite legacy applications in new languages
questions.explanation: The tech inventory supports smart budgeting, provides concrete proof when justifying upgrades, and uses automated tracking like barcodes.

questions.question: Why are future enterprise architectural views important?
choices: They replace the EA Management Plan
They document exactly what already exists today
They support resource planning, decision-making, and enterprise-wide communication
They eliminate the need for current-state documentation
questions.explanation: Future views support resource planning, decision-making support, enterprise-wide communication, and upward and downward alignment.

questions.question: A CONOPS scenario is drawn from which source to plan defensive responses and offensive initiatives?
questions.explanation: CONOPS scenarios document good and bad operating environments drawn from the SWOT Analysis so the enterprise can plan responses in advance.

questions.question: The Storytelling Technique used in CONOPS development was introduced by:
questions.explanation: The Storytelling Technique by Dr. Robert Neilson tells a short story through a central character living through future events.

questions.question: The Storytelling Technique ties a scenario to planning assumptions in three areas. Which of the following is one of them?
questions.explanation: The three areas of change are Process (how it gets done), People (who is involved), and Technology (what tools are needed).

questions.question: Which future-view artifact would track the goal 'Grow e-government service adoption 30% in 3 years'?
questions.explanation: The Balanced Scorecard is the Strategic-level future-view artifact used to track adoption goals like the 30% growth example.

questions.question: A Swim Lane Process Diagram tracing an application from Citizen to Records Office belongs to which future artifact level?
questions.explanation: Swim Lane Process Diagrams are future-view artifacts at the Business Level, which documents services and processes.

questions.question: An Activity/Entity (CRUD) Matrix defines which systems create, read, update, or delete data. At which level does this artifact belong?
questions.explanation: The CRUD Matrix is an Information-level artifact, documenting data, knowledge, and information flows.

questions.question: A System Interface Diagram showing the Permit Portal calling a Payment Gateway API belongs to which future artifact level?
questions.explanation: The Systems / Services Level documents applications and services; its artifacts include System Interface Diagrams and Web Application Diagrams.

questions.question: A Network Connectivity Diagram showing a new fiber link between City Hall and the Data Center belongs to which future artifact level?
questions.explanation: The Infrastructure Level documents physical networks, hardware, and facilities, including Network Connectivity Diagrams.

questions.question: What is the purpose of freeze periods in maintaining trustworthy future views?
choices: To prevent any new changes from ever being approved
To permanently lock the EA repository at go-live
To freeze budgets for the fiscal year
To keep current and future views frozen at regular intervals so changes are published in releases
questions.explanation: Freeze periods freeze current and future views at regular intervals (e.g., twice a year); changes accumulate for 4-5 months, then publish as a new release in month six.

questions.question: In TOGAF's view, an intermediate state that bridges the gap between baseline and target on a realistic timeline is called:
questions.explanation: Transition Architecture is one or more intermediate states that bridge the gap between baseline and target on a realistic timeline.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the four main parts of an EA Management Plan?
questions.explanation: The four parts are EA Program Management, Current Architecture Summary, Future Architecture Summary, and Glossary and References.

questions.question: Which role is responsible for managing the EA program, documentation, standards, and configuration management?
questions.explanation: The Chief Architect manages the EA program, documentation, standards, and configuration management.

questions.question: Improvements in integration, user satisfaction, or IT investment decisions are examples of which type of performance measure?
questions.explanation: Outcome measures are improvements in integration, user satisfaction, or IT investment decisions; Output measures include projects completed and scope changes.

questions.question: The number of projects completed, scope changes, or planning activities are examples of which type of measure?
questions.explanation: Output measures count things like projects completed, scope changes, or planning activities.

questions.question: What should be documented in a separate IT Security Plan instead of the main architecture summary?
questions.explanation: Sensitive security details should be documented in a separate IT Security Plan to avoid exposing vulnerabilities.

questions.question: The EA Sequencing Plan primarily ensures that:
choices: Projects occur in the correct order and dependent systems are not implemented too early
Only one technology vendor is used
questions.explanation: The EA Sequencing Plan lists projects, tasks, milestones, dependencies, and timeframes to ensure projects occur in the correct order.

questions.question: Which practice reviews and controls proposed EA changes, applies technical standards, and manages waivers?
questions.explanation: Configuration Management reviews and controls proposed changes, applies technical standards, manages waivers, and maintains version control.

questions.question: Which statement reflects the reference's analogy for EA future views?
choices: Having a full set of blueprints for modifying an existing home
Playing chess against an unknown opponent
Keeping a giant checklist of all hardware
questions.explanation: The reference analogizes future EA views to having a full set of blueprints for the modification of an existing home.

questions.question: What does the Current Architecture Summary primarily describe?
choices: The desired future direction of the enterprise
How existing resources support the organization
questions.explanation: The Current Architecture Summary describes how existing resources support the organization, including roles, strengths, weaknesses, and performance gaps.

questions.question: Which of the following is a future operating scenario mentioned in the reference?
questions.explanation: Future operating scenarios include the status quo, aggressive growth, or responding defensively to a market downturn.

questions.question: The EA Management Plan is best described as:
choices: A list of all IT project budgets
A one-time document delivered when the EA is built
A living document that guides the transition from current to future architecture
questions.explanation: The EA Management Plan directs the transition from current to future architecture and is a living document that is regularly updated.

questions.question: Why does the reference say future artifacts must use the same methods and levels as current artifacts?
choices: So future plans fit one standardized format
So change is always traceable from current to future state
So auditors can compare payroll records
So vendors can reuse existing licenses
questions.explanation: Future artifacts are built with the same planning assumptions, documentation, and modeling techniques as current views, at every level, so change is always traceable.

chapters.title: L4 — Using an Enterprise Architecture
chapters.description: Planning and project management, EAP, sequencing and prioritization, security areas, the EA repository, support tools, and integrating EA with operational IT.

questions.question: Which statement best describes what Enterprise Architecture provides to an organization?
choices: A replacement for all legacy applications
A pricing model for cloud services
A blueprint showing how parts of the organization work together
questions.explanation: EA provides a blueprint showing how different parts of an organization work together and how technology supports business goals.

questions.question: The three main areas of using an EA are commonly remembered as the sequence:
questions.explanation: The three areas are Planning & Project Management, Security, and Repository & Support Tools — remembered as Plan, Protect, and Manage.

questions.question: In the Amazon order-fulfillment example, which system processes payment after the e-commerce system receives an order?
questions.explanation: The flow is Customer Places Order -> E-Commerce System -> Payment System -> Inventory System -> Fulfillment System -> Logistics System.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Planning step in using an EA?
choices: It stores all EA diagrams and models
It converts the gap between As-Is and To-Be into a prioritized list of initiatives
It controls project scope, schedule, cost, and risk
It protects systems from unauthorized access
questions.explanation: Planning (What & Why) converts the gap between the As-Is and To-Be architecture into a list of initiatives and decides which goes first.

questions.question: EAP is defined by Spewak (1992) as:
choices: Defining the architectures needed for the business use of information and the plan to implement them
Documenting every hardware asset in the enterprise
questions.explanation: Spewak (1992) defines EAP as defining the architectures needed for the business use of information — and the plan to implement them.

questions.question: What is the guiding principle of EAP?
questions.explanation: The guiding principle is BUSINESS -> DATA -> APPLICATIONS -> TECHNOLOGY: applications manage data, technology supports applications, and everything serves a business process.

questions.question: Which choice best states the consequence of reversing the EAP order?
choices: You get a solution hunting for a problem
questions.explanation: Reverse the order and you get a solution hunting for a problem; EAP must be business-driven and data-driven, never technology-driven.

questions.question: In the 'Where we want to be' layer of EAP, which architecture is defined first?
questions.explanation: In 'Where we want to be,' data architecture comes first, then applications, then technology; these describe WHAT is needed, not how it will be coded.

questions.question: An enterprise must enforce a compliance deadline from the Data Privacy Act. Based on sequencing tests, how should this work be treated?
choices: As non-negotiable work that must be scheduled
As a dependency for every dashboard
As a pilot first, then a rollout
questions.explanation: Compliance deadlines are a sequencing test: non-negotiable work, such as the Data Privacy Act, must be scheduled.

questions.question: What is the rule of thumb the reference gives about projects that change the same system?
choices: Always run two parallel projects to save time
Never run two projects that change the same system at the same time
Only change the system when it is down
Assign both projects to the same owner
questions.explanation: The rule of thumb is to never run two projects that change the same system at the same time.

questions.question: In the 'From Architecture to Projects' process, what does Gap Analysis do?
choices: Attaches cost, benefit, and risk to each package
Places packages on a timeline with transition architectures
Compares As-Is against To-Be to find what is missing, duplicated, and obsolete
Assigns a single owner to each deliverable
questions.explanation: Gap Analysis compares As-Is against To-Be to find what is missing, duplicated, and obsolete; every project must trace back to a proven gap.

questions.question: What does a Work Package in EA planning consist of?
choices: A carved-out project scope with an assigned owner and aligned business outcome
A business case attached to cost and benefit
Two projects changing the same system
A comparison of current and target states
questions.explanation: Work Packages group related gaps into small deliverables, each with clear scope, a single owner, and one concrete outcome.

questions.question: Why does leadership fund a Business Case rather than diagrams?
choices: Because business cases are shorter to review
Because leadership funds outcomes, not diagrams
Because a business case only reports status
questions.explanation: The Business Case attaches cost, benefit, and risk to each package; leadership funds outcomes, not diagrams.

questions.question: Which role's question is 'Are we on scope, schedule, and budget?'
questions.explanation: The Project Manager / PMO cares about delivering this one project and asks whether the team is on scope, schedule, and budget.

questions.question: What is required to document an ARB deviation so a 'temporary fix' does not become permanent technical debt?
choices: A documented exception with an expiry date
questions.explanation: Any deviation needs a documented exception with an expiry date; otherwise the temporary fix becomes permanent technical debt.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the four common EA pitfalls described in the reference?
questions.explanation: The four pitfalls are ivory-tower architecture, no executive sponsor, big-bang scope, and stale artifacts.

questions.question: A business capability map describes what the firm does, such as Marketing -> Lead Generation -> Campaign Management. Which artifact class does it belong to?
questions.explanation: The Business Capability Map is a Catalog: a hierarchical decomposition of what the business does to fulfill its mission.

questions.question: Which success factor emphasizes that architecture reviews must be part of approval, not optional?
questions.explanation: Reviews at project gates are a success factor: they are part of approval, not optional.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the four main areas of security in the reference?
questions.explanation: The four areas are Data Security, Network/Technology Security, Application Security, and Physical Security.

questions.question: HR staff should only access HR data, not finance data. Which concept does this scenario illustrate?
questions.explanation: RBAC means people only get access to what they need for their job, as in the HR staff vs finance data example.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about security in enterprise architecture?
choices: Security is handled by a separate department with no EA input
Security only matters for physical hardware
Security should be considered after implementation to avoid delays
Security tasks should be part of the project timeline, not an afterthought
questions.explanation: Security should be considered while implementing the architecture, and security tasks should be part of the project timeline, not an afterthought.

questions.question: Which core repository component defines the schema, entity types, taxonomy, and relationship rules for artifacts?
questions.explanation: The Architecture Metamodel defines the underlying schema, entity types, taxonomy, and relationship rules for how artifacts connect.

questions.question: Which EA support tool capability generates dynamic visual models directly from repository data?
questions.explanation: Automated Diagramming & Layout generates dynamic visual models directly from repository data, keeping diagrams synchronized.

questions.question: Which support tool is the free, open-source, lightweight option known for ArchiMate modeling?
questions.explanation: Archi is the free, open-source, lightweight graphical modeling tool for ArchiMate modeling.

questions.question: Which EA support tool is focused on strategic IT governance and portfolio management for large enterprises and financial institutions?
questions.explanation: Software AG Alfabet focuses on strategic IT governance and portfolio management, with robust financial planning and risk alignment for large/financial firms.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the 'impact & risk analysis' capability of EA support tools?
choices: It runs traceability queries to evaluate how modifying an application impacts connected systems
It automatically draws network diagrams from cloud data
It connects via APIs to CMDBs to refresh landscape data
It provides role-based access for review boards
questions.explanation: Impact & Risk Analysis performs traceability queries to evaluate how replacing or modifying an application impacts connected systems and operations.

questions.question: In the repository governance lifecycle, what does the 'Compliance Check' stage perform?
choices: Connects to cloud platforms to refresh data
Provides approval workflows and audit trails for ARB approvals
Generates dynamic visual models from repository data
Runs traceability queries to evaluate the impact of modifying applications
questions.explanation: The Compliance Check stage performs traceability queries to evaluate how replacing or modifying an application impacts connected systems and operations.

questions.question: What does integrating the EA repository with Jira, Confluence, and CI/CD pipelines achieve?
choices: Repository data is encrypted at rest
Planned architecture guards are pushed into developer workflows
questions.explanation: SDLC & DevOps alignment ensures developer compliance; architectural guardrails are pushed directly into developer workflows.

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates CMDB & ITSM synchronization?
choices: Reconciling planned architecture with actual runtime reality via ServiceNow or AWS Config
Publishing the future view every six months
Assigning RBAC roles to HR staff
questions.explanation: Bi-directional CMDB integration reconciles planned architecture with actual runtime reality, verifying deployed assets match strategic models.

questions.question: According to the reference, what happens to IT spend when projects must trace back to business goals?
choices: Spending is capped at the infrastructure layer
IT spending increases for all departments
Duplicate and siloed systems stop being bought and built
Budgets are tied to vendor offerings
questions.explanation: Tying every peso of IT spending to a business goal stops duplicate and siloed systems from being bought and built.

chapters.title: L5 — All About Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA)
chapters.description: SOA principles, components, communication patterns, REST vs SOAP, the Enterprise Service Bus, and the evolution from monolithic to SOA to microservices.

questions.question: What is a 'service' in the context of SOA?
choices: A software component assigned a task that is reusable and modular
A database table shared across all consumers
A one-time integration between two systems
A computer program that exposes full internal logic
questions.explanation: A service is a software component assigned a task, used to make components reusable and modular for faster development.

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates the SOA principle of Reusability?
choices: A service stores state from past transactions
A payment service is used by both a website and a mobile app
A service hides its internal implementation from consumers
A large system is split into several small services
questions.explanation: Reusability means using a service in multiple parts of the system, as with the Website -> Payment Service <- Mobile App example.

questions.question: Which SOA principle requires that a service change should not affect other components using it?
questions.explanation: Loose coupling ensures changes in one service do not affect other components using it; services should also be stateless.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Abstraction principle in SOA?
choices: Consumers see the full implementation so they can debug
Clients cannot see the important logic or code behind a service
Each service manages its own database
Services communicate through a central bus
questions.explanation: Abstraction means customers and clients should not be able to see important logic or code; the app only needs the interface details.

questions.question: Which SOA component creates, maintains, and provides a service?
questions.explanation: The Service Provider creates, maintains, and provides a service, such as a company providing a Payment Service.

questions.question: Which SOA component acts as a directory of available services and how to access them?
questions.explanation: The Service Registry acts as a directory of available services, containing information about what is available and how consumers can access them.

questions.question: In which communication mode does the caller send a request and wait for an immediate reply before continuing?
questions.explanation: Synchronous communication sends a request and waits for an immediate reply before continuing; it is common with REST APIs.

questions.question: Which mechanism lets consumers locate providers at runtime instead of a hard-coded address?
questions.explanation: Service Discovery lets consumers locate providers at runtime through a service registry (e.g., UDDI) instead of a hard-coded address.

questions.question: Which statement about REST is TRUE according to the reference?
choices: It requires WS-Security for every message
It is a strict, formal messaging standard
It is an architectural style that uses standard HTTP verbs
questions.explanation: REST is an architectural style, not a strict standard, and typically uses JSON over standard HTTP verbs.

questions.question: Which statement about SOAP is TRUE according to the reference?
choices: It has built-in standards for security and transactions
It is stateless by design with no security options
It is lighter than REST and uses JSON
questions.explanation: SOAP is a strict, formal messaging standard with built-in standards for security (WS-Security) and transactions; it works over multiple transports.

questions.question: Which system type would MOST appropriately use SOAP over REST based on the reference?
choices: A banking system requiring high reliability
questions.explanation: SOAP best suits enterprise systems needing high reliability such as banking and finance, while REST suits simpler, faster web and mobile APIs.

questions.question: Which of the following is a core function of the Enterprise Service Bus (ESB)?
choices: Transformation of data formats like XML to JSON
questions.explanation: The six ESB functions include routing, transformation, protocol mediation, orchestration, monitoring & logging, and security enforcement.

questions.question: Which ESB function coordinates calls to multiple services in sequence to complete a single business process?
questions.explanation: Orchestration coordinates calls to multiple services in sequence to complete a single business process.

questions.question: Which ESB function bridges services that use different transport protocols such as HTTP, JMS, or FTP?
questions.explanation: Protocol Mediation bridges services that use different transport protocols, such as HTTP, JMS, or FTP.

questions.question: In the ESB architecture diagram, how do the Web App, Mobile App, CRM, and Legacy System communicate with the Payment, Inventory, and Shipping services?
choices: The CRM connects only to the Payment service
Each app connects directly to the service it needs
All communication flows through the ESB, and no service calls another directly
The legacy system bypasses the bus for speed
questions.explanation: All communication flows through the Enterprise Service Bus; no service calls another directly.

questions.question: Which benefit of SOA refers to teams developing, updating, and deploying individual services independently?
questions.explanation: Agility lets teams develop, update, and deploy individual services independently, drastically reducing time to bring features to market.

questions.question: Which technical advantage of SOA allows services to be written in entirely different programming languages?
questions.explanation: Technology Diversity (polyglot programming) allows services in different languages because they communicate over standard protocols like HTTP.

questions.question: If one service crashes, the rest of the application can often continue functioning. Which SOA advantage does this describe?
questions.explanation: Fault Isolation means a crash in one service often leaves the rest of the application functioning.

questions.question: Which of the following is an inherent drawback of SOA?
choices: Services cannot be reused across applications
All services must share one database
Every service must be written in the same language
questions.explanation: SOA's heavy reliance on network communication introduces unavoidable latency and complex security challenges.

questions.question: In a monolithic architecture, how does a bug in one module affect the system?
choices: It slows only the payment function
It is automatically contained by the ESB
It is isolated to that module only
It can crash the entire system
questions.explanation: In a monolithic architecture, failures are not isolated; a bug in one module can crash the entire system.

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts monolithic scaling with SOA scaling?
choices: Both scale only the specific service under load
Monoliths scale specific services; SOA duplicates the full app
Both must duplicate the entire application to scale
Monoliths duplicate the entire app; SOA scales only the services under load
questions.explanation: Monolithic architecture must duplicate the entire application to scale, while SOA scales only the specific services under heavy load.

questions.question: Which era of software architecture is described as 'one codebase, one development, simple to start, hard to scale'?
questions.explanation: The monolithic era (1990s) had one codebase and one development line: simple to start, hard to scale or change safely.

questions.question: What problem of monolithic systems forced SOA's invention?
choices: Too many independent services to manage
The entire application had to scale as one unit even if only one function was under load
Every service needed its own database
The ESB became a performance bottleneck
questions.explanation: Scalability bottlenecks occurred because the entire application had to scale as one unit, and a small change could break unrelated functionality.

questions.question: In SOA, how was interoperability between a Java service and a .NET or mainframe service achieved?
choices: By copying each other's source code
By using standardized contracts described with WSDL/SOAP
By storing all data in one shared database
questions.explanation: Standardized contracts described with WSDL/SOAP let services on different platforms interoperate.

questions.question: Which of the following is cited as a reason SOA evolved into microservices?
choices: REST APIs were not yet invented
The ESB became a single point of failure and a performance bottleneck
Services were too small and too numerous
questions.explanation: SOA growing pains included the ESB becoming a single point of failure and performance bottleneck as message volume grew.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts SOA and microservices communication?
choices: SOA uses direct calls with no middleware
Both use an ESB to mediate every message
Microservices use direct REST/gRPC calls between services
questions.explanation: SOA uses an ESB to mediate messages, while microservices make direct REST/gRPC calls straight between services.

questions.question: How does data ownership typically differ between SOA and microservices?
choices: SOA services each own private data; microservices share one database
Both share a single enterprise database
SOA often shares databases; each microservice owns its own data
Both require one table per service
questions.explanation: SOA often uses shared databases across services, while each microservice owns and manages its own data.

questions.question: Which is the modern successor to the ESB for cloud APIs?
questions.explanation: API gateways are the modern successor to the ESB, providing routing, auth, and rate-limiting for cloud APIs.

questions.question: Tools like Istio that manage service-to-service communication with retries, encryption, and observability are examples of:
questions.explanation: A service mesh (like Istio) manages service-to-service communication, echoing SOA's mediation layer with added observability.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes SOA's key takeaway about how it solved enterprise problems?
choices: SOA split logic into reusable services connected through a central ESB
SOA removed the need for any middleware
SOA made all enterprises use one coding language
SOA rebuilt every application from scratch
questions.explanation: SOA split business logic into reusable services integrated over a central ESB, letting large organizations reuse capabilities instead of rebuilding logic.

chapters.title: L6 — Integrating Technology
chapters.description: XML foundations, document structure, DTD vs XSD, XPath/XQuery/XSLT, XML parsing approaches, storage techniques, and web service technologies.

questions.question: Which phrase best describes XML according to the reference?
choices: A standard for writing data as plain text using tags that describe meaning
A compiled programming language for web servers
A file compression format for images
questions.explanation: XML is a standard for writing data as plain text, using tags that describe what the data means.

questions.question: Which property means XML tags tell you what each value is?
questions.explanation: Self-describing means tags tell you what each value is, e.g., <name> clearly labels a name value.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a listed property of XML?
questions.explanation: XML is plain text, not binary. Its four properties are self-describing, extensible, platform neutral, and data not design.

questions.question: In the sample document <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>, what is this first line called?
questions.explanation: The prolog is always the very first line and declares the XML version and encoding.

questions.question: Having exactly one outermost element with everything else inside it is a requirement for:
questions.explanation: The root element is the outermost element; there is exactly one per document and everything else sits inside it.

questions.question: In <book isbn="978-0-13-235088">, what is isbn?
questions.explanation: An attribute is written inside the opening tag in the format name="value", and its name cannot repeat on the same element.

questions.question: Which document is well-formed but NOT valid?
questions.explanation: It is well-formed (syntax correct) but not valid because <age> contains 'banana', which does not match its declared integer data type.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares DTD and XSD?
choices: DTD is written in XML and XSD uses its own syntax
Both support data types like integer and date
DTD is the modern standard and XSD is the old way
XSD supports namespaces and real data types; DTD has neither
questions.explanation: XSD is a W3C standard written in XML itself with real data types and namespace support; DTD is older, uses its own syntax, and has no data types.

questions.question: Which XML tool FINDS or locates one specific part of the document, written like a folder path?
questions.explanation: XPath finds and locates one specific part of the document, written like a folder path, without changing anything.

questions.question: Which XML tool SEARCHES XML and returns only the parts you ask for, similar to what SQL does for tables?
questions.explanation: XQuery searches XML and returns only the parts requested, like SQL for tables, e.g., querying books published after 2005.

questions.question: Which XML tool CONVERTS an XML file into a different format such as HTML, plain text, or other XML?
questions.explanation: XSLT converts XML into a different format like HTML, plain text, or other XML; the original file is never changed.

questions.question: Which parsing approach loads the whole document into memory as a tree, using memory equal to the file size?
questions.explanation: DOM loads the whole document into memory as a tree, best for small files you need to modify.

questions.question: A developer needs to read a very large XML file once, forward only, with minimal memory. Which approach fits best?
questions.explanation: SAX streams through and fires events with very little memory; it is read once, forward only, and best for very large files.

questions.question: Which approach converts XML directly into objects, best for when the schema is stable?
questions.explanation: Data Binding (JAXB) converts XML directly into objects and is best for when the schema is stable.

questions.question: The gap between the XML tree and a relational database's flat tables is called:
questions.explanation: The impedance mismatch is the gap between the XML tree structure and relational database tables.

questions.question: Invoices, purchase orders, and config files have a regular, predictable structure where order does not matter. How are these XML documents classified?
questions.explanation: Data-centric XML has a regular, predictable structure where order doesn't matter, so it suits a relational database.

questions.question: Manuals, contracts, and articles have irregular, mixed content where order matters. These are best stored in:
questions.explanation: Document-centric XML with irregular content and order sensitivity is best stored in a native XML database.

questions.question: Which XML storage technique breaks the tree into rows and columns, making the original document no longer exist?
questions.explanation: Shredding breaks the XML tree into rows and columns, enabling fast joins and reports, but the original document no longer exists.

questions.question: Which storage approach keeps the whole document in one column while also copying key fields into normal columns?
questions.explanation: The hybrid / XML column approach keeps the whole document in one column and copies key fields into normal columns, trading fidelity and speed at the cost of duplication.

questions.question: Which standardized format family does the reference associate with global interbank payments?
questions.explanation: ISO 20022 is the standardized format for global interbank payments.

questions.question: Which standardized format family is used for healthcare and clinical data?
questions.explanation: HL7 / CDA is the standardized format family for healthcare and clinical data.

questions.question: What was UDDI created for?
choices: To define the XML vocabulary for banking
To encrypt SOAP messages in transit
To help organizations publish and discover web services
questions.explanation: UDDI (Universal Description, Discovery, and Integration) was a directory where businesses could publish and discover web services.

questions.question: What does WSDL provide for a SOAP web service?
choices: A runtime registry of available instances
A technical contract describing services, operations, and access
questions.explanation: WSDL acts like a technical contract describing what services are available, what operations they support, and how they can be accessed.

questions.question: Which WS-* specification adds authentication, encryption, and message integrity to SOAP messages?
questions.explanation: WS-Security adds authentication, encryption, and message integrity to SOAP messages, often paired with SAML assertions.

questions.question: Which WS-* specification ensures messages are still delivered correctly even over unstable networks?
questions.explanation: WS-ReliableMessaging ensures messages are delivered correctly even over unstable networks.

questions.question: In web services integration, which approach uses a central process that directs how services interact from the top down?
questions.explanation: Orchestration relies on a central process that directs how different services interact, coordinating them from the top down.

questions.question: Which integration approach lets services communicate directly with one another in a peer-to-peer manner with no single controlling process?
questions.explanation: Choreography lets services communicate directly peer-to-peer with no single controlling process.

questions.question: Why does the reference describe XML as the 'lingua franca' of enterprise integration?
choices: It is the fastest binary format
It is the official standard of one vendor
It requires a specific operating system
It is a vendor-neutral, self-describing common language any platform can interpret
questions.explanation: XML acts as a vendor-neutral, self-describing common language with explicit tags that any hardware or software platform can interpret.

questions.question: How does XSLT help bridge differing enterprise schemas without modifying original databases?
choices: It locks the database while the schema changes
It renames database tables for the new schema
It converts supplier PO formats to canonical enterprise standards
It drops incompatible rows from the database
questions.explanation: XSLT transforms supplier PO formats to canonical enterprise standards, mapping incompatible field names automatically.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a well-formed and a valid XML document?
choices: Valid means well-formed AND follows a schema
Valid requires every attribute to be repeated
questions.explanation: Well-formed documents meet syntax rules; valid documents are well-formed AND follow a schema (only allowed elements present, values matching types).

chapters.title: L7 — Integrating Applications
chapters.description: Application integration styles, real-time vs batch integration, legacy system integration, enterprise integration architectures, and integration patterns.

questions.question: What is the goal of Application Integration according to the reference?
choices: To replace every independent application with a single system
To create a seamless flow of information and processes across systems
To store all data in one shared spreadsheet
To make all applications use the same programming language
questions.explanation: The goal is a seamless flow of information and processes across systems, reducing or eliminating manual data transfer.

questions.question: Which of the following is a reason application integration matters?
choices: It reduces manual data entry and human error
It keeps data in isolated departmental silos
It requires staff to copy data between systems
questions.explanation: Integration eliminates data silos, reduces manual entry and human error, improves accuracy, and speeds up decision-making.

questions.question: A website connects directly to a payment gateway without an intermediary. Which integration style does this represent?
questions.explanation: This is point-to-point integration: a direct, custom-built connection between two systems, generally not reusable.

questions.question: What is the main limitation of point-to-point integration as more systems are added?
choices: It eliminates the need for APIs
It requires a central integration engine
It becomes difficult to manage and scale, leading to 'spaghetti' architecture
It stops working entirely after five systems
questions.explanation: Point-to-point integration leads to a tangled 'spaghetti' architecture that is difficult to manage and scale as systems grow.

questions.question: In hub-and-spoke integration, how do the systems connect to each other?
choices: Systems connect through a peer-to-peer mesh
Systems exchange flat files on a shared drive
Each system connects directly to every other system
Each system connects to a central hub that routes communication
questions.explanation: In hub-and-spoke, each system connects to the central hub, reducing the total number of connections.

questions.question: A bank uses middleware to connect core banking, a mobile app, and an ATM network using XML and JSON. Which layer does this example illustrate?
questions.explanation: An ESB acts as a common communication backbone routing and transforming messages between systems with different formats and protocols.

questions.question: A ride-sharing app uses Google Maps, Stripe, and Twilio through well-defined interfaces. Which integration approach does this use?
questions.explanation: API-based integration lets independent components communicate through well-defined APIs, as with the ride-sharing example.

questions.question: Which integration timing best suits a stock trading platform that updates balances right after every trade?
questions.explanation: Real-time integration syncs data immediately; stock trading updates balances right after every trade.

questions.question: A payroll system syncs attendance data overnight in large volumes. Which timing approach does this use?
questions.explanation: Batch integration collects and transfers data at scheduled intervals, reducing processing overhead and system load.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common challenge in application integration?
choices: Fewer points of failure as systems grow
Data format mismatches that require transformation
Decreased security risk from fewer entry points
questions.explanation: Common challenges include data format mismatches, security risks from more entry points, system downtime/dependency, and growing complexity.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the core approaches to legacy system integration?
questions.explanation: The five core approaches are API Wrapping, Middleware Connectivity, ESB, iPaaS, and ETL & Data Synchronization.

questions.question: Why do businesses still keep and integrate legacy systems?
choices: Because they already run on modern APIs
To avoid the massive expense and risk of rebuilding core databases
Because legacy systems are the most scalable
To eliminate the need for staff training
questions.explanation: Businesses keep legacy systems for cost savings, avoiding the huge expense and risk of rebuilding core databases.

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts legacy integration with implementing a new system?
choices: Legacy integration minimizes disruption; new systems risk downtime during transition
Legacy systems are more easily customizable than new ones
New systems require less training than legacy ones
New systems offer lower upfront cost than integration
questions.explanation: Legacy integration causes minimal disruption, while new system implementation carries high risk of downtime and requires extensive training.

questions.question: Which of the following is a challenge of integrating legacy systems?
choices: Data inconsistency due to proprietary formats
questions.explanation: Legacy databases use proprietary formats requiring complex translation logic, causing data inconsistency challenges.

questions.question: Which incremental modernization pattern minimizes operational risk when migrating legacy systems?
questions.explanation: The Strangler Fig pattern is an incremental approach that minimizes operational risk during legacy migration.

questions.question: Which pattern protects a legacy system from a new system's data model changes?
questions.explanation: An Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) protects a legacy system from a new system's data model changes.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key objective of Enterprise Integration (EAI)?
choices: Data consistency to establish a single source of truth
questions.explanation: EAI objectives include data consistency, system interoperability, business process automation, and real-time visibility.

questions.question: Which enterprise integration architecture lets subscribing services react asynchronously in near-real time to published events?
questions.explanation: EDA publishes event messages to an enterprise broker, letting subscribing services react asynchronously in near-real time.

questions.question: Which enterprise integration pattern inspects incoming message contents and routes data based on business rules?
questions.explanation: A Content-Based Router inspects incoming message contents and routes data to the correct destination based on business rules.

questions.question: Which pattern converts data payloads between incompatible structures, such as XML to JSON or EDI to SQL?
questions.explanation: A Message Translator converts data payloads between incompatible structures and formats.

questions.question: Which pattern delivers messages from a single sender to multiple subscribed systems simultaneously without direct coupling?
questions.explanation: A Publish-Subscribe Channel delivers messages from a single sender to multiple subscribed systems simultaneously.

questions.question: Which of the following is a business benefit of enterprise integration?
choices: Higher chances of building duplicate tools
Operational efficiency that cuts manual entry and error
questions.explanation: Operational efficiency cuts manual entry and error; other benefits include agility, scalability, and cost optimization.

questions.question: Which is a challenge in enterprise integration?
questions.explanation: Challenges include high architectural complexity, single point of failure, data security and compliance, and resource and skill requirements.

questions.question: Which best practice enforces that components depend on contracts rather than each other's internals?
questions.explanation: Enforcing loose coupling is a best practice; related practices include API standardization, centralized monitoring, and high availability design.

questions.question: Which integration strategy is described as having a 'connection count that grows quickly'?
questions.explanation: Point-to-point connections grow quickly in number and are hard to manage at scale.

questions.question: An organization needs many systems to coordinate through a central layer with better visibility. Which strategy fits best?
questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke / ESB centralizes routing and policies, improving visibility and manageability in larger environments.

questions.question: Which benefit of API-based integration allows the same API to serve multiple clients?
questions.explanation: API-based integration is reusable — the same API can serve multiple clients while auth is controlled at the interface.

questions.question: In event-driven integration, who publishes an e.g. 'Order Created' event?
questions.explanation: The Event Producer publishes events (like 'Order Created'), and the Event Broker publishes/routes them to consumers.

questions.question: What does iPaaS (Integration Platform as a Service) provide?
choices: A cloud-hosted toolset connecting applications and data across cloud and on-premises environments
A relational database storing documents in XML columns
A local firewall appliance protecting the internal network
A manual file exchange service running on a shared drive
questions.explanation: iPaaS provides cloud-hosted tools for connecting applications and data across cloud and on-premises environments with reusable connectors.

questions.question: When choosing an integration strategy, large scheduled transfers best suit which approach?
questions.explanation: The reference states large scheduled transfers suit batch-oriented approaches, while real-time needs favor APIs or event-driven flows.

chapters.title: L8 — Enterprise Integration
chapters.description: Enterprise integration fundamentals, XML integration best practices, web services and APIs, SOAP vs REST, security and authentication, and the Service-Oriented Enterprise.

questions.question: What is the key idea behind Enterprise Integration according to the reference?
choices: Replacing existing systems with one platform
questions.explanation: The key idea is that integration is about connecting, not replacing, existing systems.

questions.question: Why do companies need integration even though each system works on its own?
choices: Because data silos cause duplicate entries and inconsistent records
Because every system uses a common database
Because manual copying is always accurate
Because systems already share consistent records
questions.explanation: Many systems don't talk to each other, producing data silos, duplicate entries, and inconsistent records that integration removes.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of enterprise integration?
questions.explanation: Benefits include real-time data sharing, faster decisions, reduced manual work/errors, cost savings, and better customer service.

questions.question: Which failure mode results from one field using different tags across systems?
questions.explanation: Inconsistent data — the same field with different tags across systems — causes mapping to break silently.

questions.question: Which practice helps maintain clear structure in XML?
choices: Nesting every element five levels deep
Using short cryptic tags to reduce file size
Using meaningful names like <shippingAddress> and a logical hierarchy
questions.explanation: Clear structure uses meaningful names (e.g., <shippingAddress>, not <sa>) and a logical hierarchy with flat, DRY content.

questions.question: Which layered validation is recommended before accepting an XML payload?
choices: File size and read speed only
Well-formed syntax, schema (XSD) check, required fields and types
questions.explanation: Recommended validation is layered: well-formed syntax, schema (XSD) check, matching tags and root, and required fields and types.

questions.question: Which security measure protects XML data in transit?
questions.explanation: SSL/TLS (HTTPS) encrypts the XML in transit; the reference says to protect every hop.

questions.question: Why should seemingly harmless external entities in XML be disabled?
choices: To reduce the number of tags
questions.explanation: Blocking XML attacks includes disabling external entities and capping size/depth to prevent injection and disclosure.

questions.question: For large XML collections, which performance approach is recommended?
choices: Paginate or stream large payloads, and gzip when useful
Embed all data into one attribute
questions.explanation: Performance guidance: send only necessary data, keep XML reasonably sized, paginate/stream large collections, and gzip when useful.

questions.question: What should an error response provide for good XML error handling?
questions.explanation: Error handling should give clear, specific, actionable feedback rather than a generic error code.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly describes authentication vs authorization?
choices: Authentication asks 'what can you do?'; authorization asks 'who are you?'
Authentication asks 'who are you?'; authorization asks 'what can you do?'
Both ask who the user is
Both ask what the user can do
questions.explanation: Authentication = 'who are you?'; Authorization = 'what can you do?'

questions.question: Which statement about REST and SOAP is TRUE in the L8 comparison?
choices: SOAP is slower because of heavier messages
REST must always use XML and JSON together
questions.explanation: SOAP is a protocol with built-in security and heavier XML messages, making it slower; REST is a lighter architectural style.

questions.question: Which example best fits where SOAP should be used over REST?
questions.explanation: SOAP fits banking, enterprise, and government use, such as interbank transfer systems; REST suits web and mobile apps.

questions.question: Which mechanism is commonly used for authentication in modern APIs?
questions.explanation: Authentication approaches include API keys, OAuth 2.0, JWT, and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).

questions.question: Which practice helps prevent SQL injection and XSS?
questions.explanation: Input validation prevents SQL Injection and XSS; rate limiting and firewalls prevent abuse and DDoS.

questions.question: Which mechanism used by tools such as RabbitMQ and Kafka supports reliability?
questions.explanation: Reliability includes redundant/failover systems, retries, message queuing (RabbitMQ, Kafka), and health monitoring with SLA.

questions.question: Which of the following is a performance optimization for web services?
questions.explanation: Performance optimizations include caching, load balancing, data compression (GZIP), pagination, and CDNs.

questions.question: Which of the following is a web services best practice from the checklist?
questions.explanation: Best practices include using HTTPS always, proper authentication, validating inputs, designing for failure, and versioning APIs like /api/v1/.

questions.question: What is a Service-Oriented Enterprise (SOE)?
choices: An enterprise that runs all systems on one mainframe
An enterprise with no system integration
An enterprise that only uses SOAP web services
An enterprise that connects business systems through reusable services
questions.explanation: An SOE connects business systems through reusable services, focusing on integration, flexibility, and reuse of existing systems.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five main components of a Service-Oriented Enterprise?
questions.explanation: The five components are Service Provider, Service Consumer, Service Registry/Broker, Service Interface, and Enterprise Service Bus.

questions.question: Which SOE component defines how a service can be accessed?
questions.explanation: The Service Interface defines how a service can be accessed.

questions.question: Which of the following is the FIRST step in building the Service-Oriented Enterprise?
choices: Design services based on specific business functions
Identify business processes that need integration
Integrate, test, and monitor the services
questions.explanation: The first step is to identify business processes that need integration, then identify existing systems that can be reused.

questions.question: Which key characteristic is used to describe Service-Oriented Architecture?
choices: Loose coupling, reusability, interoperability, and scalability
questions.explanation: SOA's key characteristics include loose coupling, reusability, interoperability, and scalability, with services communicating through standard interfaces.

questions.question: In the school example, how are the student information, payment, library, and learning platforms connected?
choices: Through services, sharing data across systems
questions.explanation: The school connects student info system, payment system, library system, and learning platform through services.

questions.question: Which document format is associated specifically with SOAP?
questions.explanation: SOAP uses XML only, while REST supports JSON, XML, and plain text.

questions.question: Which API type offers flexible querying so clients request only what they need?
questions.explanation: GraphQL offers flexible querying, letting clients request only what they need.

questions.question: Which statement about XML integration failure modes is TRUE?
choices: Malformed values never corrupt downstream records
Undocumented schema changes quietly break trading partners
questions.explanation: Compatibility issues — undocumented schema changes — quietly break trading partners; unvalidated input opens the door to injection and disclosure.

questions.question: What does the reference warn about processing sensitive data in XML?
choices: Store credentials directly in element names
Share access with the maximum privilege
Leave PII visible in tags for debugging
Mask or encrypt PII at rest and in tags
questions.explanation: Best practice guards sensitive data by masking/encrypting PII at rest and in tags, and follows least privilege.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the L8 role of SSL/TLS encryption?
questions.explanation: HTTPS/SSL/TLS encryption protects data in transit; WS-Security provides message-level security for SOAP.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of building an SOE?
choices: Reuse of services reduces development time and costs
Systems become tightly coupled to one vendor
Every service requires its own duplicate data
questions.explanation: Benefits include better integration and flexibility, reduced development time and costs via reuse, and easier maintenance and expansion.

encyclopedia.definition: A detailed, step-by-step approach that describes how an Enterprise Architecture program is established, developed, managed, maintained, and used within an organization.
A structured set of tools, models, and guidelines used to organize and design an enterprise's architecture, providing a common language and structure.

A 6x6 classification schema (36 cells) developed by John Zachman in 1987; columns are What/How/Where/Who/When/Why and rows are Planner, Owner, Designer, Builder, Sub-Contractor, Enterprise. It is a reference checklist, not a methodology.
The Open Group Architecture Framework; helps organizations design, plan, implement, and manage enterprise architecture using the ADM cycle.

Architecture Development Method: the TOGAF method that identifies business requirements, analyzes current architecture, designs the target, identifies changes, plans implementation, and manages/reviews.
Federal Enterprise Architecture Framework, developed by the U.S. Federal Government to organize and manage enterprise architecture, supported by six reference models (PRM, DRM, SRM, BRM, ARM, TRM).
Performance Reference Model: measures how well an organization and its IT systems achieve strategic goals and desired outcomes.
Data Reference Model: defines how data is categorized, described, shared, and managed across the enterprise.
Security Reference Model: defines security-related capabilities, controls, and requirements for protecting enterprise systems and information.
Business Reference Model: describes the organization's business functions, services, and activities.
Application Reference Model: organizes IT services and application components that support business functions.
Technical Reference Model: provides a common structure for technologies, platforms, and technical standards used by the enterprise.
An EA methodology from Gartner that views EA as a continuous process of change and improvement, focused on business strategy, stakeholders, and outcomes rather than technology alone.
The foundation of the EA framework; defines the organization's business strategy, governance, structure, and key business processes.
The structure and management of an organization's logical and physical data assets and data management resources.
A blueprint for the individual applications' deployment, their interactions, and their relationships to core business processes.
The hardware, software, and network infrastructure that provides the hosting and runtime environment for applications.
An architectural work product that describes an aspect of the architecture - deliverables, documents, diagrams, models, matrices, and catalogs produced throughout the EA lifecycle.
A hierarchical list or inventory of things that answers 'What inventory do we have?' e.g., Application Portfolio Catalog.
A grid showing the relationship between two or more architectural elements, answering 'How do elements relate?' e.g., Application-to-Function Matrix.
Visual representations of architecture components and their topology or dynamics, answering 'What does the structure or flow look like?'
The rigorous link across Business -> Data -> Application -> Technology layers so every technical asset maps back to a business need; enables impact analysis, cost optimization, and strategic agility.
The current architectural view; a complete snapshot of a company's technology and processes right now, serving as the baseline and blueprint.
A standard format request used to update systems smoothly; archiving these requests creates a history guide for developers.
A visual modeling technique that clearly shows inputs and outputs, the Controls (rules), and the Mechanisms (tools) of a process.
A diagram that defines how different parts of the business relate, e.g., how a Buyer connects to a Listing.
Documentation of IT resources expected to be active several years ahead, used for resource planning, decision support, and enterprise-wide communication.
A Concept of Operations scenario documenting good and bad operating environments drawn from the SWOT Analysis to plan defensive and offensive initiatives in advance.
Dr. Robert Neilson's technique of writing a short story through the eyes of a central character living through future events, tied to assumptions in Process, People, and Technology.
A strategic-level future-view artifact used to track goals such as 'Grow e-government service adoption 30% in 3 years.'
A business-level future artifact tracing a process such as an application from Citizen -> Apply -> Portal -> Submit -> Records Office.
An Activity/Entity matrix (Create, Read, Update, Delete) at the Information level, e.g., 'Permit Record' created by Intake, updated by Reviewer, deleted by Records Admin.
Freezing current and future views at regular intervals (e.g., twice a year); changes accumulate for 4-5 months and publish as a new release in month six.
The current, 'as-is' structure of the enterprise; the starting point for any transformation in TOGAF.
One or more intermediate states that bridge the gap between baseline and target on a realistic timeline.
The desired future state: capabilities, processes, and technologies aligned to strategic goals.
A living document guiding the transition from the current architecture to the desired future architecture; coordinates IT projects, resources, standards, governance, and implementation.
The person who manages the EA program, documentation, standards, and configuration management.
Performance measures reflecting improvements in integration, user satisfaction, or IT investment decisions.
Performance measures counting number of projects completed, scope changes, or planning activities.
A plan listing projects, tasks, milestones, dependencies, and timeframes to ensure projects occur in the correct order.
Reviews and controls proposed EA changes, applies technical standards, manages waivers, and maintains documentation and version control.
A structured approach to organizing an organization's business, data, applications, and technology, providing a blueprint of how parts work together.
The planning discipline (Spewak, 1992) defined as 'defining the architectures needed for the business use of information — and the plan to implement them.'
BUSINESS -> DATA -> APPLICATIONS -> TECHNOLOGY: applications manage data, technology supports applications; EAP is business-driven and data-driven, never technology-driven.
Comparing the As-Is against the To-Be to find what is missing, duplicated, and obsolete; every project must trace back to a proven gap.
A grouping of related gaps into small deliverables, each with clear scope, a single owner, and one concrete outcome.
Attaches cost, benefit, and risk to each work package; leadership funds outcomes, not diagrams.
Holds checkpoints at initiation, design, and before go-live; each review ends in approved, approved with conditions, or rejected.
A common EA pitfall: beautiful models nobody follows.
Role-Based Access Control: people only get access to what they need for their job, e.g., HR staff can't touch finance data.
Controlling who can see, change, or take the organization's data; one of the four main areas of security.
The master storage facility for all architectural assets, models, principles, and guidelines; maintains single-source-of-truth visibility for As-Is, To-Be, and Transition states.
A repository component defining the schema, entity types, taxonomy, and relationship rules governing how architectural artifacts connect.
A repository component that catalogs real-time operational views, target blueprints, and active roadmap transitions.
An EA support tool capability that generates dynamic visual models from repository data, keeping diagrams synchronized with data.
An EA support tool capability that runs traceability queries to evaluate how modifying an application impacts connected systems and operations.
An EA tool focused on Application Portfolio Management for agile, cloud-native enterprise IT; known for fast SaaS setup and automated landscape discovery.
An EA tool known for deep modeling and system specs with comprehensive support for TOGAF, ArchiMate, UML, and SysML.
A free, open-source, lightweight graphical modeling tool for ArchiMate modeling used in educational and lean teams.
Configuration Management Database (e.g., ServiceNow, AWS Config); bi-directional integration reconciles planned architecture with actual runtime reality.
