Service-Oriented Architecture: an approach in software development where applications are created using services.
A software component assigned a task; reusable and modular, with a clearly defined interface that hides internal implementation.
Using a service in multiple parts of the system, e.g., Website -> Payment Service <- Mobile App, preventing duplicate functionality.
Proper documentation and description of a service so changes in one service do not affect others; services should be stateless.
Clients and customers should not see important logic or code; they only need to know how to request and what response to expect.
Dividing a large system into smaller, manageable services, each with its own responsibility.
The SOA component that creates, maintains, and provides a service.
The application or system that requests and uses a service.
A directory of available services containing information about what is available and how consumers can access them.
Representational State Transfer: an architectural style, not a strict standard; uses HTTP verbs GET/POST/PUT/DELETE, typically JSON, stateless.
Simple Object Access Protocol: a strict, formal messaging standard with messages as XML envelopes and built-in WS-Security and transactions.
Middleware that sits between services handling routing, translation, and message delivery so no service knows another's technical details.
An ESB function that coordinates calls to multiple services in sequence to complete a single business process.
An ESB function that bridges services using different transport protocols, such as HTTP, JMS, or FTP.
An ESB function that converts data formats between systems, such as XML and JSON.
Tools like Istio that manage service-to-service communication, adding retries, encryption, and observability; echoes SOA's mediation layer.
The modern successor to the ESB: routing, auth, and rate-limiting for cloud APIs, centralizing cross-cutting concerns.
eXtensible Markup Language: a standard for writing data as plain text using tags that describe what the data means.
The first line of an XML document, declaring version and encoding, e.g., <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>.
The outermost element of an XML document; exactly one per document, with everything else inside it.
Metadata written inside an opening tag in the form name="value"; a name cannot repeat on the same element.
XML with correct syntax: exactly one root, every tag closed, no overlapping tags, quoted attribute values, case-sensitive names.
Well-formed XML that also follows a schema: only allowed elements appear, required elements present, values match data types.
Document Type Definition: the old schema language written in its own syntax, with no data types and no namespace support.
XML Schema Definition: the modern W3C-standard schema language written in XML itself, with real data types and namespace support.
XML tool that FINDS one specific part of a document, written like a folder path, e.g., /library/book/title.
XML tool that SEARCHES XML and returns only requested parts, similar to SQL for tables.
XML tool that CONVERTS an XML file into a different format (HTML, text, or XML); the original file is never changed.
Loads the whole XML document into memory as a tree; best for small files you need to modify.
Streams through XML firing events; read once, forward only, very little memory; best for very large files.
Your code asks for the next piece when ready; same efficiency as SAX but you control the loop and can skip sections.
The gap between the XML tree and a relational database's flat tables; storing one in the other is never free.
An XML storage database where the document itself is the unit of storage, e.g., eXist-db, BaseX, MarkLogic.
An XML storage technique breaking the tree into rows and columns; fast joins and reports, but the original document no longer exists.
Web Services Description Language: an XML-based language that acts like a technical contract describing a SOAP service.
Universal Description, Discovery, and Integration: a directory where businesses and applications could publish and discover web services.
The WS-* specification adding authentication, encryption, and message integrity to SOAP messages, often with SAML assertions.
The WS-* specification ensuring messages are still delivered correctly even over unstable networks.
Enabling independently designed applications to communicate, exchange data, and work together as a coordinated system.
A direct, custom-built connection between two systems, generally not reusable; leads to 'spaghetti' architecture at scale.
A central hub (integration engine) manages and routes communication between multiple systems, reducing total connections.
Connecting and enabling communication between older, outdated systems and newer systems or technologies.
An incremental modernization pattern that minimizes operational risk when migrating legacy systems.
A pattern that protects a legacy system from a new system's data model changes.
Enterprise Application Integration: linking separate applications, databases, and hardware platforms across an organization to work together as a coordinated ecosystem.
Systems publish event messages to an enterprise broker, letting subscribing services react asynchronously in near-real time.
An integration pattern that inspects incoming message contents and routes data to the correct destination based on business rules.
An integration pattern that converts data payloads between incompatible structures, e.g., XML to JSON, EDI to SQL.
An integration pattern delivering messages from a single sender to multiple subscribed systems simultaneously without direct coupling.
Integration Platform as a Service: cloud-hosted tools for connecting applications and data across cloud and on-premises environments.
Linking different IT systems, applications, and data sources so they can work together and share data seamlessly; about connecting, not replacing, existing systems.
The practice of exchanging structured data between systems using XML as a common format, with best practices for structure, validation, security, performance, and errors.
An API approach offering flexible querying so clients request only what they need.
Verifying who a user is: 'who are you?'
Determining what a user can do: 'what can you do?'
An enterprise that connects business systems through reusable services, focusing on integration, flexibility, and reuse.
The SOE component that defines how a service can be accessed.
The standardized format family for global interbank payments.
The standardized format family for healthcare and clinical data.
Standardized format families for B2B supply chains.
